cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK II
The assembly at Ithaca;\nPenelope's web; Telemachus sails by night.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,\nthe dear son of Odysseus rose up from his bed,
put on his clothes, slung his\nsharp sword about his shoulder,
bound the beautiful sandals beneath his shining feet,\nand came out of his bedroom looking like a god.
At once he ordered the clear-voiced heralds\nto cry the long-haired Achaeans into assembly.
The heralds cried the summons,\nand the men gathered quickly.
And when they were assembled, all in one gathering,\nhe went to the assembly, the bronze spear in his palm,
not alone: two swift dogs followed with him,\nand Athena poured a wondrous grace upon him.
All the people gazed at him in wonder as he came;\nhe sat in his father's seat, and the elders gave way.
Then the hero Aegyptius was first to speak among them,\na man bent with age, who knew things past numbering.
His own dear son had gone with godlike Odysseus\nin the hollow ships to Ilium of the fine horses —
Antiphus the spearman; the savage Cyclops killed him\nin his hollow cave, and made of him his last supper.
Three other sons he had:\none kept company with the suitors —
Eurynomus — and two worked their father's lands always.
Even so, he could not forget the one:\ngrieving, mourning him.
In tears for him, he now addressed the assembly:
"Hear me now, men of Ithaca, hear what I say.
Never once has our assembly met, has our council sat,\nsince noble Odysseus went away in the hollow ships.
Who has gathered us now? On whom has need come down so hard,\nwhether among the young men or the elder-born?
Has he heard some news of the army coming home which\nhe might tell us plainly, having learned of it first?
Or is there some other public\nmatter he would open and argue?
A good man he seems to me, a blessed one. May Zeus
accomplish for him some good —\nwhatever his heart desires."
So he spoke, and the dear son of Odysseus\nrejoiced at the omen of the word,
and sat no longer: desire took him to speak.
He stood in the middle of the assembly,\nand the scepter was put in his hand
by the herald Peisenor, a man of clear-headed counsel.
Then he spoke, turning first to the old man:
"Old sir, that man is not far off —\nyou shall see for yourself —
who called the people: it is I;\ngrief comes down hardest on me.
I have heard no news of the army coming home which I\nmight tell you plainly, having learned of it first,
nor is there other public matter I would open and argue:
it is my own need, the evils fallen on my house —\ntwofold. I have lost my noble father, who once was king
among you here, and he was gentle as a father;\nand now something far greater, which will soon tear apart
my whole house utterly and destroy my living altogether.
Suitors have set upon my mother — against her will —\nthe own dear sons of the men who here are noblest,
and they shrink from going to the house of her father
Icarius, so that he might set his\ndaughter's bride-terms himself
and give her to whom he will,\nwhoever comes and pleases her.
Instead they haunt our house day after day,\nslaughtering our oxen and our sheep and our fat goats,
feasting and drinking the fire-bright wine
with no reckoning. And the most of it\nis wasted. For there is no man here
such as Odysseus was, to beat ruin away from the house.
We are not the men to beat it\nback — believe me, ever after
we would be pitiable men, and unschooled in fighting.
Beat it back I would, if only the strength were in me!
For what is done here is past all bearing; past all\ndecency my house is ruined. Feel the outrage yourselves;
feel shame before the peoples who are our neighbors,
those who dwell around us;\nand dread the wrath of the gods,
lest in fury at evil deeds they\nturn them back on your heads.
I beg you — by Olympian Zeus, and by Themis,\nwho dissolves the assemblies of men and seats them —
hold off, friends! Leave me alone to waste away in my\nbitter grief. Unless perhaps my father, good Odysseus,
in malice did the strong-greaved Achaeans harm,\nand in requital you do me harm in malice,
egging these men on. Better for me by far if it were\nyou yourselves devouring my treasures and my herds:
were you the ones eating,\nthere might one day be repayment,
for then we would go up and down\nthe town pressing our claim,
demanding our goods back, until all was given over.
Instead you heap on my heart pains past any remedy."
So he spoke in anger,\nand dashed the scepter to the ground,
bursting into tears. And pity took hold of all the people.
Then all the rest stayed silent, and no one\ndared to answer Telemachus with hard words;
Antinous alone made him this answer:
"Telemachus, high talker, temper past\nrestraining — what a thing you have said,
smearing us with shame!\nYou would love to hang the blame on us.
But it is not the Achaean suitors who are at fault:
it is your own dear mother, whose cunning has no equal.
For it is the third year now, and the fourth soon coming,
that she has cheated the heart in the Achaeans' breasts.
She gives hope to all, and makes promises to every man,
sending out messages — while her mind wills otherwise.
And here is another trick her heart devised:
she set up a great loom in the halls and wove at it,
fine-threaded, beyond all measure wide,\nand told us straightway:
'Young men, my suitors — since noble Odysseus is dead,\nwait, though you burn for my wedding, till I finish
this cloth — let my spinning not be wasted on the wind —\na shroud for the hero Laertes, against the day
the ruinous doom of death that lays men low will take him:
let no Achaean woman in the land hold it against me
that a man who won so much should\nlie without his winding-sheet.'
So she spoke, and our proud hearts were persuaded.
Then every day she wove at the great loom,\nand every night she unwove it by torchlight.
Three years her trick escaped us,\nand she kept the Achaeans persuaded;
but when the fourth year came, as the seasons rolled on,\nthen one of her women, who knew it all, told us,
and we caught her unweaving the shining web.
So she finished it — against her will, under force.
Now the suitors give you this answer,\nso that you may know it
in your own heart, and all the Achaeans know it:
send your mother away. Command her to marry\nwhichever man her father bids, and who pleases her.
But if she goes on tormenting the sons of the Achaeans —
minding in her heart the gifts Athena gave her beyond\nall women, skill in beautiful work, and a noble mind,
and cunning past anything we\nhear of even in the women of old,
the fair-braided Achaean women of the time before,\nTyro and Alcmene and Mycene of the lovely crown:
not one of them had thoughts to match Penelope's —\nyet this one thought of hers was not well thought.
For just so long will men devour\nyour living and your goods
as she holds to this purpose the gods are setting\nnow in her breast. Great fame she is making
for herself — and for you,\nthe ache of a squandered living.
We are not going to our estates, or anywhere else,\nbefore she marries whichever Achaean she will."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Antinous, there is no way I can\nthrust out of the house, unwilling,
the one who bore me, who raised me —\nwhile my father, somewhere on earth,
lives or is dead. And it would go hard with me to pay back
Icarius so much, if of my own\naccord I send my mother home.
From her father I would suffer evil; and heaven would add
more, since my mother, leaving the house, would call\ndown the loathed Furies; and the blame of men would be
upon me. No: I will never speak that word.
As for you — if your own hearts feel any shame at it,
get out of my halls. Go busy yourselves with other feasts,
eating your own goods, moving from house to house.
But if this seems to you the\nbetter thing, the more profitable,
that one man's living be destroyed and nothing paid,
then carve away. And I will cry\nto the gods who live forever,
in hope that Zeus may grant\ndeeds of requital come to pass:
then you would die inside this house,\nand nothing paid for you."
So spoke Telemachus. And Zeus of\nthe wide voice sent him two eagles,
flying from on high, from a mountain peak.
For a while the two flew on with the breath of the wind,\nclose by one another, wings at full stretch;
but when they came dead over the many-voiced assembly,
they wheeled there, beating their wings thick and fast,
and glared down on all their heads,\nand death was in their gaze;
then they ripped with their talons\nat each other's cheeks and throats
and shot away rightward, over the houses and the town.
The men were astonished at the birds their eyes had seen,
and turned over in their hearts\nwhat this would bring to pass.
And among them spoke the old hero Halitherses,\nMastor's son, who surpassed all men of his day
in reading birds and speaking what fate intends.
With good will toward them he spoke to the assembly:
"Hear me now, men of Ithaca, hear what I say —\nthough to the suitors above all I declare it:
on them a great wave of ruin is rolling. For Odysseus
will not be long parted from\nhis people; already, somewhere
near, he is planting death and slaughter for these men,
every one; and evil will come on many of the rest of\nus who live in clear-skied Ithaca. Long before that,
let us think how to stop them — or let them stop themselves:\nthe sooner the better, for their own sake.
I prophesy as no novice; I know my art.
And for that man too I say it is all coming home,\nall I told him when the Argives went up into Ilium
and Odysseus of the many designs went with them.
I said that after long suffering, his companions all lost,\nunknown to everyone, in the twentieth year
he would come home. And now it is all being accomplished."
Then Eurymachus, Polybus' son, answered him:
"Old man, off with you —\ngo home and prophesy to your children,
lest some evil overtake them in days to come.
In this I am a far better prophet than you.
Plenty of birds go back and forth\nbeneath the rays of the sun,
and not all of them are fate. As for Odysseus:
he is dead, far away — and how I\nwish that you had perished with him.
You would not then be spouting all this prophecy,\nor whetting the anger of Telemachus —
angling for some gift for your\nhousehold, should he offer one.
But I will tell you this, and it will be accomplished:
if you, who know so many things grown old with you,
talk a younger man around with words and stir him to fury,
for the man himself, first, it will go the harder,
and in any case he will accomplish\nnothing for all these words;
and on you, old man, we will lay a fine that in the paying
will gall your heart: and the pain of it will be hard.
And to Telemachus, before you all, my own advice is this:
let him command his mother to\ngo back to her father's house.
There they will make the marriage\nand set out the bride-gifts,
very many, all that should follow a beloved child.
Not before, I think, will the sons of the Achaeans quit
their courting — a grinding courtship.\nWe fear no one, not at all;
no, not Telemachus, for all his stream of words;\nnor do we care a whit for prophecy, old man, that you
mouth to no accomplishment —\nit only makes you the more hated.
His goods will be devoured as badly as ever, and never\nmade good, so long as she puts the Achaeans off about
her marriage. And we, waiting all our days,\nrival one another for her excellence, and do not go after
other women, fit brides for any of us."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Eurymachus, and all you other haughty suitors:
I plead with you no further; I say no more of this.
The gods know it now, and all the Achaeans.
But come, give me a fast ship and twenty companions\nto carry me on a journey there and back again.
For I am going to Sparta and to sandy Pylos to\nask after the homecoming of my long-gone father,
in hope some mortal man will tell me,\nor I may hear the Rumor
that comes from Zeus, which most\nof all carries word among men.
If I hear my father is alive and homeward bound, then,\nground down as I am, I could hold out one more year;
but if I hear that he is dead, that he is no more,\nthen I will come back to my own dear fatherland
and heap his burial mound,\nand over it pay the death-rites,
very many, as is fitting,\nand give my mother to a husband."
So he spoke, and sat down. And there rose among\nthem Mentor, the companion of blameless Odysseus,
to whom, going aboard his ships,\nhe had entrusted his whole house —
that all should obey the old man,\nand he keep everything safe.
With good will toward them he spoke to the assembly:
"Hear me now, men of Ithaca, hear what I say.
Let no sceptered king ever again be willingly kind\nand gentle, or know the right way in his heart;
let him rather be harsh always, and act outrage —\nsince no one remembers godlike Odysseus
among the people he ruled, and he was gentle as a father.
It is not the lordly suitors I begrudge, not really,
for their deeds of violence\nwoven in an evil-scheming mind:
they lay their own heads on the wager when they devour
by violence the house of Odysseus,\nsaying he will come home no more.
It is the rest of the people I\nam angry at — the way you all
sit there dumb, and never fasten on them with words\nand stop them: the suitors few, and you so many."
Then Leocritus, Evenor's son, answered him:
"Mentor, wrecker, brain gone wandering —\nwhat a thing you have said,
urging them to stop us. It is heavy work to fight\nwith men over a feast — men who outnumber you at that.
Why, if Ithacan Odysseus himself came in on us\nand found the lordly suitors feasting in his house
and set his heart on driving them out of the hall,\nhis wife would have no joy of his coming, however
she has ached for him:\nright there he would meet an ugly death,
if he fought men who outnumbered him.\nWhat you have said misses the mark.
Come now — people, scatter, each man to his own work.
As for this one, Mentor and\nHalitherses can speed his journey,
being companions of his father's house from the beginning.
Though I think he will sit here a\nlong while yet, gathering his news
in Ithaca; that voyage he will never make."
So he spoke, and dissolved the assembly on the instant.
They scattered, each man to his own house, and the\nsuitors went off to the house of godlike Odysseus.
But Telemachus walked apart, to the sand-beach of the sea,
washed his hands in the gray\nsalt water, and prayed to Athena:
"Hear me, you who came yesterday, a god, into our\nhouse, and bade me go by ship over the misted sea
to ask after the homecoming of my long-gone father.
All of it the Achaeans grind to a halt —\nthe suitors most of all, in their evil overbearing pride."
So he prayed, and Athena came to him, close at hand,\nin the likeness of Mentor, both his body and his voice,
and lifting her voice she spoke winged words to him:
"Telemachus, you will be no\ncoward from this day, and no fool,
if any of your father's brave force is instilled in you —
such a man he was for making good both deed and word.
Then this journey of yours will be no\nidle errand, and not unaccomplished.
But if you are not his son, his and Penelope's,
then I have no hope you will\naccomplish what you set your heart on.
Few sons, in truth, turn out the equals of their fathers:
the most are worse; a few are\nbetter men than their fathers.
But since you will be no coward\nfrom this day, and no fool,
and the cunning of Odysseus has not wholly failed in you,\nthere is every hope you will accomplish this work.
So now let the suitors' plotting and scheming go —\nmindless men, with neither sense nor justice in them:
they know nothing of the death and the black doom that\nstands close by them, to destroy them all in a day.
The journey you have set your\nheart on will not be long delayed —
such a companion am I, out of your father's house:
I will fit out a fast ship for you, and come along myself.
You go back to the house now, and move among the suitors;
make ready provisions, and stow them all in vessels —
wine in two-handled jars, and barley meal, the marrow\nof men, in tight-sewn skins. And I, through the town,
will gather willing companions,\nand quickly. There are ships
in plenty in sea-circled Ithaca, new ships and old:
I will look them over for you and choose the best,\nand we will rig her fast and launch her on the wide sea."
So spoke Athena, daughter of Zeus. And no longer then
did Telemachus linger, once he\nhad heard the voice of the god.
He went on his way to the house,\nhis heart heavy within him,
and found the lordly suitors there in the halls,\nskinning goats and singeing fat hogs in the courtyard.
Antinous came laughing straight at Telemachus,\nclamped a hand on his, and spoke a word, and named him:
"Telemachus, high talker,\ntemper past restraining — let no other
evil trouble your breast, no other deed or word.
Just eat with me, and drink, the way it used to be.
The Achaeans will see to all those things of yours —\na ship and picked oarsmen — so you may come the sooner
to holy Pylos, after news of your proud father."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Antinous, there is no way, among you in your insolence,\nto eat my supper quietly and take my ease in peace.
Is it not enough that all this\nwhile, suitors, you carved up
my goods, so many and so fine, while I was still a child?
Now — when I am grown, and hear the talk of other men\nand understand it, and the spirit swells inside me —
I will try to hurl an evil doom upon you,\nwhether I go to Pylos or stay here in this land.
But go I will, and the journey I\nspeak of will be no idle errand —
a passenger on another's ship,\nsince master of ship or oarsmen
I am not to be. That, no doubt,\nseemed the more profitable to you."
He spoke, and wrenched his hand from Antinous' hand,
easily. And through the house the\nsuitors busied themselves with the feast,
and they mocked him and needled him with words.
And thus would one of the arrogant young men say:
"No question — Telemachus is planning our murder!
He will bring back avengers from sandy Pylos,\nor else from Sparta, since he is so terribly set on it.
Or maybe he means to go to Ephyra, that rich plowland,\nto fetch home poisons that eat the life away,
and drop them in the wine-bowl, and destroy us all."
And thus would another of the arrogant young men say:
"Who knows? Maybe he too, once aboard the hollow ship,
will wander far from his people\nand be lost — just like Odysseus.
And that would double our work, wouldn't it:
we would have to divide all his\ngoods among us, and the house itself
hand over to his mother — hers,\nand the man who marries her."
So they talked. But he went\ndown to his father's storeroom,
high-ceilinged and broad, where gold and bronze lay piled,
and clothing in chests, and fragrant oil in plenty;\nand there stood great jars of old wine, sweet to drink,
holding the unmixed divine drink within them,\nranged in order along the wall — against the day Odysseus
might come home even after all his pains.
Doors were on it, close-fitted, bolted fast,\ndouble doors; and a woman-steward was there night and day
who guarded it all with her mind's deep knowledge:
Eurycleia, daughter of Ops, Peisenor's son.
Telemachus called her into the storeroom and spoke to her:
"Nurse, come — draw me off wine in two-handled jars,\nthe sweet wine, the finest-tasting after that
which you keep, thinking of him —\nthe luckless one — if from somewhere he should come:
Zeus-born Odysseus,\nhaving slipped past death and the dooms.
Fill twelve, and fit them all with lids.
And pour me barley meal into well-sewn skins:
twenty measures of mill-crushed barley grain.
Keep this to yourself. And let it all stand gathered:
in the evening I will fetch it, when at last my\nmother climbs to her upper room and thinks of sleep.
For I am going to Sparta and to sandy Pylos to ask\nafter my dear father's homecoming, if I may hear of it."
So he spoke, and his dear nurse Eurycleia wailed aloud,\nand grieving she spoke winged words to him:
"Why, dear child, why has this thought come into\nyour mind? Where would you go across the wide earth,
an only son, and beloved? He is dead far from home —\nZeus-born Odysseus, in some strangers' country.
And these men, the moment you are gone,\nwill plot evils behind you,
to kill you by treachery and\ndivide all this among themselves.
Stay here instead, sitting on\nwhat is yours. There is no need
to suffer evils on the barren sea, and go wandering."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered her:
"Take heart, nurse. This plan is not without a god.
But swear you will not breathe a word to my dear mother\nbefore the eleventh day has come, or the twelfth,
or she misses me herself and hears that I am gone —\nso she will not mar her lovely skin with weeping."
So he spoke, and the old woman\nswore the great oath of the gods.
And when she had sworn and made an end of the oath,
straightway she drew off wine for him in two-handled\njars and poured him barley meal into well-sewn skins;
and Telemachus went back to the\nhall to move among the suitors.
Then the goddess thought of one\nthing more, gray-eyed Athena.
In the likeness of Telemachus she\nwent everywhere through the town,
and standing beside each man she spoke her word,\nbidding them gather at evening by the fast ship.
Then she asked Noemon, the shining son of Phronius,\nfor a fast ship; and he promised it gladly.
The sun went down, and all the ways grew dark.
Then she hauled the fast ship down to the sea,\nand stowed in her all the gear that well-benched ships carry,
and moored her at the harbor's edge.\nAround her the brave companions
gathered in a body, and the goddess\nset each man's heart on fire.
Then the goddess thought of one\nthing more, gray-eyed Athena.
She went on her way to the house of godlike Odysseus,\nand there she poured sweet sleep over the suitors,
addled them as they drank,\nand knocked the cups from their hands.
They stumbled off to sleep through the town,\nand sat no longer, for sleep was falling on their eyelids.
But to Telemachus gray-eyed Athena spoke,\ncalling him out in front of the well-settled halls,
in the likeness of Mentor, both his body and his voice:
"Telemachus, your strong-greaved companions are already\nsitting at the oars, waiting on your word to start.
Come, let us go; let us not hold the journey long."
So speaking, Pallas Athena led the way swiftly,\nand he followed in the footsteps of the god.
And when they had come down to the ship and the sea,\nthey found the long-haired companions on the beach,
and the sacred strength of Telemachus spoke among them:
"Come, friends, let us fetch\nthe provisions: everything now
stands gathered in the hall. My mother has heard nothing,\nnor the slave-women either; one alone was told."
So speaking he led the way, and they went with him.
They carried everything down and stowed it in the\nwell-benched ship as the dear son of Odysseus commanded.
Then Telemachus went aboard, Athena going before him;
she sat down in the stern of\nthe ship, and close beside her
sat Telemachus. And the men cast off the stern-lines
and came aboard themselves and\ntook their places at the oarlocks.
And gray-eyed Athena sent them a following wind,\na fresh West Wind, singing over the wine-dark sea.
Telemachus shouted to his companions, commanding them
to lay hands on the rigging, and they heard his urging:
they raised the pine mast and stepped\nit inside the hollow mast-box,
set it up and made it fast with the forestays,
and hauled up the white sails by\nthe well-twisted ox-hide ropes.
The wind bellied out the middle of the sail, and the wave
hissed dark and loud around the keel as the ship went on,\nand she ran down the waves, making her way.
Then, when they had lashed the\ntackle down the fast black ship,
they set up mixing-bowls crowned brim-full with wine\nand poured to the deathless gods who are forever,
and beyond all others to the gray-eyed daughter of Zeus.
All night long, and into the dawn, the ship cut her way.
